title: Byte Streams: FileInputStream and FileOutputStream
learningObjectives: Read raw file data using FileInputStream and byte arrays
Write binary data using FileOutputStream and byte buffers
Detect end-of-stream using the documented negative-one result
Copy files while writing only the number of bytes actually read
Close input and output streams safely after every operation

understand.concept: FileInputStream reads bytes and FileOutputStream writes bytes. The read method returns -1 at end of stream. For larger files, use a byte buffer.
understand.whyItMatters: Byte streams preserve raw bytes and are appropriate for binary data such as images, archives and arbitrary file copies. Correct buffering and end-of-stream handling prevent truncated output and unnecessary one-byte I/O operations.
understand.analogy: A byte stream is like moving sealed numbered packets: the program copies each byte without interpreting it as a letter or character.
understand.analogyLimit: Bytes do not inherently represent text. Decoding arbitrary bytes as characters without knowing the encoding can corrupt or misinterpret data.

explain.narrative:
## Byte-oriented file input and output

`FileInputStream` reads the raw bytes stored in a file, while `FileOutputStream` writes raw bytes to a destination. Use this pair for binary formats such as images, archives and audio. A byte stream does not interpret character encoding; it transfers byte values exactly.

## Read one byte or read a block

The single-byte `read()` method returns an int from 0 through 255, or -1 when the stream reaches end-of-file. Do not store the result in a byte before checking for -1, because -1 is the end marker rather than a data byte.

For efficient copying, pass a non-empty byte array to `read(buffer)`. The returned count is the number of bytes filled in this read. The final read may fill only part of the buffer, so write exactly `count` bytes with `write(buffer, 0, count)`; writing the entire buffer can append stale bytes from a previous iteration.

## Copy files safely

Open source and destination streams with try-with-resources. Decide whether an existing destination should be replaced or appended; the default FileOutputStream constructor truncates an existing file. If preserving the old destination matters, write to a temporary file and replace only after a successful copy.

## Verify binary integrity

Do not compare binary files by printing them as text. Compare byte arrays or use a checksum, and test empty input, a file smaller than the buffer, a file larger than the buffer and data containing zero-valued bytes. Handle IOException and ensure both streams close when a read or write fails.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var in = new java.io.ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[]{65,66,67})) { System.out.println((char)in.read()); } } }
examples.explanation: Reads the first byte and interprets its ASCII value as a character for demonstration.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var out = new java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream()) { out.write(new byte[]{65,66}); System.out.println(out.size()); } } }
examples.explanation: Writes two bytes to an output stream.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var in = new java.io.ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[]{65,66,67})) { int b; while((b=in.read())!=-1) System.out.print((char)b); } } }

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var in = new java.io.ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[]{1,2,3,4})) { byte[] buffer = new byte[2]; int count=in.read(buffer); System.out.println(count + ":" + buffer[1]); } } }
examples.explanation: Reads a block of bytes into a buffer.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println(new java.io.ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[0]).read()); } }
examples.explanation: Confirms that an empty stream immediately reports end-of-stream.

practise.guidedTask: Copy a temporary binary file with FileInputStream and FileOutputStream using a fixed-size byte buffer. Compare source and destination bytes.
practise.independentTask: Implement a byte-copy method that loops until read returns -1, writes only the bytes actually read and closes both streams safely.
hints: Check for -1 before treating a single-byte read result as data; read() returns int for this reason.
For read(byte[]), write only the returned count, not the full buffer capacity.
Test empty, short, multi-buffer and zero-byte binary files; compare bytes or checksums rather than decoded text.
practise.challenge: Test an empty file, a file smaller than the buffer, a file larger than the buffer and binary bytes containing zero values.

questions.prompt: What does FileInputStream.read() return at end of stream?
questions.explanation: FileInputStream.read() returns -1 when no more bytes are available; check this sentinel before treating the int as file data.

questions.prompt: Which API writes raw bytes to a file?
questions.explanation: FileOutputStream writes raw byte values to a file and does not interpret them as characters.

questions.prompt: Why use a byte buffer when copying a large file?
options: It transfers multiple bytes per read/write operation
It converts all binary data into text
It prevents the destination from existing
questions.answer: It transfers multiple bytes per read/write operation
questions.explanation: A byte buffer transfers multiple bytes per I/O call, reducing repeated low-level operations during a large copy.

questions.prompt: Which resource declaration ensures a stream is closed?
questions.explanation: Declaring the stream in a try-with-resources header causes Java to close it when the statement exits, including exceptional exits.

questions.prompt: Why should arbitrary binary data not be decoded as text without a format?
options: The bytes may not represent valid text in the assumed charset
Text readers automatically repair all binary formats
questions.answer: The bytes may not represent valid text in the assumed charset
questions.explanation: Arbitrary binary bytes may not form valid text in an assumed charset, so verify binary copies as bytes or with a checksum.
